title: Repairing a split chair back splat with hide glue
subtitle: Glue a split chair back splat with liquid hide glue, cramp flat while setting, and clean up the dried joint
excerpt: How to repair a split chair back splat using hide glue. Covers cleaning the joint surfaces, preparing hot hide glue or liquid hide glue, applying the glue, cramping the joint flat, checking for wind, and cleaning squeeze-out.
sourceNotes: Traditional furniture restoration practice, public domain. UK furniture conservation and restoration trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: An animal-protein glue made from rendered connective tissue, available as dried pearls or flakes that are dissolved in water and heated to 60 to 70 degrees Celsius before use. It sets by cooling and gelling rather than by chemical cure. Hide glue is reversible with heat and moisture, which is essential for conservation work, and it provides excellent glue-line strength along the grain of timber.

The central decorative vertical panel in the back frame of a chair, running between the top rail and the seat rail. In antique chairs it is typically shaped timber, pierced or carved; in simpler chairs it is a flat or slightly curved board. A split in the splat commonly runs along the grain.

content.text: split along the grain is an ideal candidate for
: reversible, strong on long-grain joints, and compatible with the original finish. INTERMEDIATE: the joint must be dry, clean, and cramped flat while the glue sets.

Remove any old dried glue from the joint faces using a wooden scraper or fine chisel. The wood fibres must be fully exposed: residual old glue prevents adhesion. Blow or vacuum out any loose fibres and dust. Allow the wood to dry at room temperature before applying fresh glue.

Soak the pearl hide glue in cold water for 30 minutes at a ratio of 1 part pearls to 1.5 parts water by weight. Heat in a double boiler or glue pot to 60 to 65 degrees Celsius, stirring until fully dissolved. The glue should run off the brush like thin cream. Do not overheat: temperatures above 70 degrees degrade the glue strength. Work quickly as hide glue gels as it cools.

Brush a thin, hot coat of hide glue onto both joint faces immediately before cramping. Press the joint together and apply the sash cramp across the width of the splat, using clamping blocks to spread the pressure and prevent cramping marks on the surface. Check the joint is not in wind (twisted): if the two edges of the splat are not in the same plane, apply a second cramp diagonally across the twist.

Wipe all squeeze-out from the joint faces immediately with a damp cloth. Leave the cramp in place for at least one hour at room temperature. Allow 24 hours before removing the cramp and loading the joint. Clean any remaining glue residue from the face with a slightly damp cloth: dried hide glue is water-soluble and cleans up easily.

attrs.symptom: Joint opens again after the cramp is removed
attrs.cause: The glue cooled and gelled before the joint was fully closed, or the joint surfaces were oily from an old wax or oil finish.
attrs.fix: Warm the joint gently with a heat gun to soften the old glue, separate the joint, clean both faces, and re-glue. Degrease with naphtha before applying glue if the wood is oily.

attrs.symptom: Glue residue shows as a dark stain on the wood surface after finishing
attrs.cause: Squeeze-out was not wiped away while wet.
attrs.fix: Sand the stained area lightly with fine abrasive and re-apply the finish. Hide glue stains that are sealed under finish are not structurally significant.
